A procession of youthful figures appears, crowned with flowers; in the half-light before dawn, their torches bring out the whiteness of the garments that drape them. From what festivities, from what celebrations in the night, are they returning? The torches go out like the stars, and the figures vanish into the distance.

Thirty years later, some young people asked Goethe what the poem would have become had he finished it, and what it would have revealed about the mysterious brotherhood's work. His reply explains the intention embodied in HUMANUS: the fully HUMAN Man, the centre of a constellation of distinct, representative personalities. Drawn to him by a deep affinity and by their aspirations, they can reach their fullest development only by gathering around him.

Following Brother Marcus on his journey, the reader or listener would have come to understand that each particular religion reaches its richest flowering and fulfilment by drawing nearer to this supreme Guide and mediator—even, ultimately, by becoming perfectly identified with him. The different ages would have been represented by twelve figures so distinctive that they would have made one thing clear: wherever the recognition of God and virtue appears, however surprising its form, it always deserves the fullest reverence and love.

What Goethe's spiritual vision embraced in this mystical gathering, then, was the complete course of humanity's true direction. Humanity may follow that direction unknowingly, even against its own wishes, and misunderstand it. It may also reject it, just as it may reject its invisible Guides, knowing nothing of them and perhaps no longer even suspecting the order of reality to which they belong. That is why Goethe, who had very probably conceived the poem under the influence of the Grail tradition, said in his reply that readers should orient themselves toward a kind of “ideal Montserrat.” The poem was intended to lead the human being—its hero, Humanus—to discover happiness and repose “on the summit of his own Montserrat.”

Instead of “Mont-Serrat,” another tradition allows us to say “Mont-Salvat.” The essential meaning remains the same. The very idea of this “inner Montserrat” brings us back to the mountain of Qâf, which belongs at once to the soul and the cosmos. Brother Marcus's ascent is the same as that of Suhrawardi's mystical heroes. And there is more. According to Goethe, the twelve knights who meet in chapter beneath the emblem of the Rose Cross, and among whom Brother Marcus finds himself, each represent one of humanity's religions.

Each comes closer to perfection as it draws nearer to the figure who is their common centre, the thirteenth. Now consider what we read in Ibn Abî Jomhûr, one of the greatest Shiite theosophers, who here follows very closely the esoteric teaching of Ibn 'Arabî: “The Twelfth Imam is the pole and the Imam of this age. In him every Imam and every pole converge, from East to West, from Earth to Heaven [...].

“For the world continues to be preserved as long as this Perfect Man remains within it [...]. This shows us that in the twelve Imams, from first to last, all religions are made manifest in both their outward and their inward meaning, and with them all the perfections of the visible and invisible orders. If they were to be lacking, if they were absent, the universe would cease to exist and return to its origin. For through them everything began, and to them everything returns.”

There is a striking correspondence, in what can be grasped of their spiritual meaning, between Goethe's vision of the twelve knights and the vision of the complete assembly, or pleroma, of the twelve Imams. In each case the central figure is also the thirteenth, because he expresses the unity and completion of the Twelve. This is true of the Friend of God of the Oberland at the final gathering of the twelve Friends, and of Humanus surrounded by the twelve knights of the Rose Cross.

The Twelfth Imam, too, is in a sense the thirteenth, because he comes after the eleven preceding Imams and the Seal of the Prophets. There is, moreover, a perfect correspondence between him and the Seal of the Prophets: he is, as it were, Muhammad returned to life. He gathers the entire pleroma into himself. He is the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat—the bond of divine friendship, Gottesfreundschaft—and the Perfect Man in whom the cycle of appearances of the Muhammadan Light (Nûr mohammadî) in this world reaches its final fulfilment. Shiite ontology certainly places the pleroma of the Imams on a higher level than the twelve at the Oberland gathering or the twelve at Montserrat.

Yet this does not weaken the correspondence between these symbolic forms. Both Western assemblies are manifestations, at the level of the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world, of that same pleroma of the Twelve.
Let us draw together the essential features shared by these mystical assemblies.

First comes the idea of spiritual Guides who belong to a higher world, or who have been chosen and brought together through the commands or arrangements of beings from such a world. Their assembly of twelve is then an image—and indeed a complete image—of the spiritual cosmos, whose energies decisively affect humanity.

Each time, the number of those assembled suggests a correspondence with particular dimensions of the cosmos. The first gathering of seven Friends in the High Country corresponds, like the groups of seven Imams in Ismailism, to the seven planetary spheres: the seven metals, the seven colours of light, and the seven notes of the scale.

The gatherings of twelve correspond to the twelve zodiacal constellations in the heaven of the fixed stars. Shiite teachings concerning the Imams see those constellations as visible symbols of the twelve Imams' “dwelling places,” themselves represented as twelve “Veils of Light” (and twelve millennia) within which the “Muhammadan Light” resides. In a similar way, each of Goethe's twelve knights is an alchemical, or “philosophers',” dwelling place for the hero Humanus.

The twelve gather around a mysterious figure: the Friend of God, Rulman Merswin's secret companion; Humanus, in Goethe's poem; or the Twelfth Imam, in Shiite teachings about the Imams. In every case, the mysterious figure at the centre of the pleroma of Twelve has resolved to enter occultation (ghaybat). His companions must not search for him in some location within the physical world. Their search would be in vain. (We may recall the knights of Kay Khosraw here.) In each case, occultation—the passage into a state of “invisible presence”—is announced as the secret of a new cycle. And the idea of this new cycle is inseparable from the idea of spiritual chivalry.

Whether the new cycle can unfold depends on the fidelity of the Twelve in the High Country and the Twelve on Montserrat. This is the final message sent to the Johannites of the Green Island, and the message Brother Marcus receives on the summit of Montserrat.

The future and fate of humanity depend on their knightly service, although humanity knows nothing of it; for through them it still maintains contact with the spiritual worlds. They hold back the horror of the storm that threatens to destroy the human in humanity, until the Human Being has attained full spiritual stature. Together with their leader, they form the keystone of mystical hierarchies that never cease working upon human existence, yet are known to only a few. Ordinary people know nothing of them; most do not even suspect that they exist.

And yet if these Guides ceased to be, humanity would be engulfed by catastrophe. Conversely, it is through them that humanity fulfils its destiny from one cycle to the next. They alone know the hidden pattern—the “cipher”—of its secret history. Nothing of this can be traced in the outward, material facts studied by sociology or by philosophies concerned only with outward appearances, though those disciplines still claim to deduce, using only the categories available to them, what they call the “meaning of history.”

We find the same signs in the famous conversation in which the First Imam initiated his disciple Komayl ibn Ziyâd into the secret of gnosis and its unbroken line of transmission (silsilat al-'irfân). Ghaybat—occultation, with its consequences and the ethical demands it imposes—is a fundamental theme of Imamite theosophy. Just as the Chosen One and Guide in Goethe's poem bears the name Humanus, meaning the human in the fullest, most complete sense, so the Twelfth Imam, the “Awaited Imam,” is the Perfect and complete Human Being (Insân kâmil, Anthropos teleios).

A dramatic aura surrounds each of the twelve Imams. Each is perceived as the brief appearance in this world of a figure belonging to another, and each appearance has inevitably encountered the rejection of the multitude and the opposition of established political and religious powers. The Twelfth Imam's particular aura is that of his ghaybat: his invisible presence in this world, the anonymity into which human incomprehension has driven him.

Here lies the central paradox of Shiite religious feeling: beauty and perfection are offered to humanity, only to be rejected or reviled. From that paradox arises the feeling at the heart of walâyat, the feeling that shapes the life of the person called, in classical Persian texts, a javânmard—best translated as a “spiritual knight,” a knight of faith. What Brother Marcus is to Humanus, every Shiite believer must be to the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam.

Through faith and fidelity, the believer's own person and life can become the beginning of the Imam's “unconcealment.” The sincerity of the wish spoken whenever the Imam is mentioned—“May God hasten the joy of his coming!”—must be shown in the believer's ethos, in the way that person lives. Each must become the Imam's fellow worker, helping to prepare his return and manifestation (a feeling powerfully expressed in the pilgrim's prayer we shall quote at the end; there are many others). This idea and this way of life have remained deep within Iranian spirituality since the distant age of Zoroaster's preaching.

In Shiite theology, the manifestation that will announce the Resurrection has its exact counterpart in the Zoroastrian idea of Frashkart: the transfiguration or renewal of the world. The Zoroastrian ethic of the Fravartis and the ethic of the javânmard together express the whole message of spiritual chivalry handed down by Iran. We have suggested its profound, hidden harmony with the message of the Johannite knights of the Green Island and that of Goethe's knights of the Rose Cross.
But there is more to be said.
2. The Abrahamic Tradition and Spiritual Chivalry (javânmardî)

The Persian word javânmardî, which we have just used, is one of the key terms of Persian mystical vocabulary. It corresponds to the Arabic fotowwat, a word for a way of life found across wide regions of Islamic civilization. Wherever it appears, it bears a distinctly Shiite imprint, and for good reason. We might call fotowwat the ethical category par excellence. It gives spiritual meaning to human fellowship, to the bond between companions, and it was therefore the inspiration behind the many guilds of crafts and other occupations that spread throughout the Islamic world.

Those in Turkish lands have received particular attention from scholars. Those in Iran have so far been studied much less (editions of several texts are now being prepared there). This is paradoxical, since the Iranian world was very probably where the idea first took shape. Every scholar of the subject has sensed that the origins of fotowwat must be sought as far back as ancient, pre-Islamic Persia.

Within the Islamic world, fotowwat presented itself as arising from Sufism, and as it gave shape and structure to the fellowship of occupational associations, it brought a sense of “chivalrous service” into every activity of life, complete with ritual, initiations, grades, bonds of brotherhood, secrecy, and the like. We ought to compare this with a similar phenomenon in the West: the “Order of the Companions of the Holy Duty of God,” the Devoirants, who knew—and still know—“the Orient and the Line” (l'Orient et le Trait).

Would establishing contact with them be something new, or would it restore a bond lost for centuries? There is much to say, and much to do, on this subject. Naturally we cannot explore here the vast spread of this tradition, still less its inevitable distortions. Our concern is first to clarify what the word means, and then to identify the essential nature of the practice: how Shiite thinkers understand the origin of fotowwat and the relationship between its manifestations, the cycle of prophecy, and the cycle of walâyat.

Our principal source will be the Fotowwat-Nâmeh, written in Persian by Hoseyn Kâshefî, the great Iranian preacher and spiritual teacher of the fifteenth century (d. 910 AH / 1504–05 CE). His book treats the knowledge of fotowwat chiefly as “a branch of the knowledge of Sufism and tawhîd,” the affirmation of divine unity.

The word itself cannot really be explained without bringing in the very essence of what it names. Our author makes this clear in detail, supporting his account with many quotations. The Arabic fatâ corresponds to the Persian javân (Latin juvenis); mard-e javân means a young man, roughly between sixteen and thirty years of age. The Arabic fotowwat corresponds to the Persian javânî (Latin juvenitas), meaning youth. That is the literal sense, referring to bodily age.

In its technical, spiritual sense, however, the word describes a youth over which time has no power, because it has been won back from time and from the hardening that time brings. It is the youthfulness proper to spiritual beings, the qualities awakened in us by the idea of youth. When the mystic—the pilgrim or wayfarer (sâlik, a word that exactly conveys our idea of homo viator, the human being on a journey)—has gradually freed himself, on his “inward” path, from the passions of the bodily soul, he reaches the station of the heart: the inward, true human being.

In that very place he has entered the dwelling of youth (manzala-ye javânî), of youth that has come to stay. The Persian compound javânmard (Arabic fatâ) therefore means someone in whom human perfections, spiritual energies, and the soul's inward powers (qowwatha-ye ma'nawî) have become fully active. It also describes a person whose shining qualities and exemplary conduct set that person apart from the ordinary run of humankind.

Hence the abstract noun javânmardî (Arabic fotowwat) means—and here we hear again the contrast so characteristic of the Iranian vision of the world—“the manifestation of the light of humanity's original nature (nûr-e fitrat-e insânî), and the victorious mastery of that light over the darkness of the bodily soul, so that a human being, cured of every vice, possesses every moral excellence.” This is the soul's essential youthfulness.

To explain the essence of fotowwat, then, is to return to the fundamental idea of fitrat, humanity's original nature: what the human being was when, at the beginning, the act of existence—its dimension of light—sprang from the creative Act. At the same time, what that being would be, its own distinctive essence, was determined by the “tone” of its response to the question A-lasto? (“Am I not [your Lord]?”; Quran 7:171). That response governs the whole understanding of the human being.

In its complete purity, as we have seen, it includes a threefold testimony: to divine Unity, to the mission of the prophets, and to the walâyat of the Imams. This already points to the bond between fotowwat and walâyat. It also explains why fotowwat is often used as another name for îmân, complete faith in the Shiite sense. Purity of soul is the sign of a return to that original nature.

Thus when Moses asked—our author refers to the Torah here, without specifying a passage—“Lord, what is fotowwat?” the answer came: “To return to God the soul pure and unstained, just as humanity received it in trust.” This alludes to the Quranic theme of the “trust entrusted,” on which we encountered Haydar Âmolî's masterful commentary. It is in this sense that one can say: “Fotowwat is a light emanating from the spiritual world.

“When this light shines into a being and flows through that being, angelic qualities (sifât-e malakî) and the characteristics of the Malakût become manifest within. Every satanic disposition, every habit of the animal nature that stifles the soul imprisoned in the flesh, is banished.”

Of the many definitions of fotowwat, Hoseyn Kâshefî pays particular attention to those given in turn by the Imams, except the Twelfth. As the Seal of fotowwat, the Twelfth Imam has the task of bringing to fulfilment and completion everything his predecessors have taught about it.

Having established its essential link with fitrat, we shall retain here only the words of the Third Imam, Hosayn ibn 'Alî, the martyr of Karbala: “Spiritual chivalry (fotowwat, javânmardî) means remaining faithful to the pre-eternal covenant”—the covenant made in response to A-lasto?—“and walking with firm steps on the great road of the eternal religion (dîn qayyim), the road called the straight path (sirât mostaqîm).” Such is the javânmard, the knight of faith.

We are also told that the knowledge of fotowwat is “a branch of the knowledge of Sufism and tawhîd.” This necessarily brings fotowwat into close relation with the threefold distinction we have encountered throughout this work: sharî'at (the Law, religion in its outward or literal form), tarîqat (the mystical path), and haqîqat (the spiritual truth personally realized).

The inward meaning of “poverty” (faqr) in Sufism is an ontological poverty: the utter dependence of a created being for its existence. One bears witness to this poverty by affirming, as Haydar Âmolî does, the realized spiritual truth—the haqîqat—of tawhîd understood at the level of being itself.

If fotowwat points, in its essence, to fitrat, humanity's original, pre-existent nature, the forms in which it appears cannot be separated from the cycles of prophecy and walâyat as Shiite teaching understands them. There is, in fact, a cycle of fotowwat.

How does it relate to the two cycles of prophecy and walâyat that we have already described at length (above, Book I)? Hoseyn Kâshefî, summing up the teachings of earlier writers, identifies three decisive moments: fotowwat originates with Abraham, who brings it into manifestation as something distinct from the tarîqat, the Sufi path; its pole (qotb), or spiritual centre, is the First Imam; and its Seal (khâtim), the figure who brings it to completion, is the Twelfth Imam.

Everyone agrees that the prophetic mission, nobowwat, began in this world with Adam, after he had left Paradise. In that role, Adam could only be the man of the sharî'at, the revealed Law. The inward meaning of prophecy, later to be called walâyat, was entrusted to his son Seth, the first Imam of Adam's period. “Adam had to spread the carpet of the sharî'at”—that is, of the Law and the religion of legal obligations—“in the arena of human existence subject to the Law ('obûdîyat), while Seth spread the carpet of the mystical path (tarîqat).”

The original distinction was thus established. While Adam's other sons took up various occupations, Seth devoted himself entirely to divine service, “a mystical weaver who wove no garment other than that of Sufism.” (We may recall here the place of Seth among the Sethian Gnostics, and his identification with Zoroaster, while Ismaili gnosis gives the name Melchizedek to the Imam of the first three periods of the prophetic cycle.) In short, Seth was the first Sufi, and there are beautiful legends to explain how this came to be.

In his person fotowwat was part of the tarîqat. Neither for Seth nor for his followers was there any distinction between the mystical path, or Sufism, and fotowwat: the tarîqat itself set the measure of fotowwat, and both shared the same garment, the khirqa, the cloak symbolizing a Sufi's initiation and consecration.

We learn next that in Abraham's time, people no longer had the strength to wear the khirqa. A whole group admitted this to Abraham and asked him to show them a path by which they could still follow their longing and calling to become people of God. (Here we may remember the concern shared by the Friend of God and Rulman Merswin: the age of cloisters was over, and another kind of spiritual foundation had to be imagined.) Our authors pass down the same story, rich in imagery.

Abraham took this group aboard the ship of the tarîqat. He launched the ship upon the open sea of haqîqat, realized spiritual truth, and brought it to the island of fotowwat, where they made their home. (Here we naturally think of the voyage toward the Imam's Green Island.) The meaning is very subtle. Once aboard the ship of Sufism, the only way to disembark in the midst of the ocean of haqîqat is to reach the island of fotowwat.

Spiritual chivalry is inseparable from Sufism in its origin. Sufism is the path toward realizing haqîqat, the spiritual truth; by that very fact it is the way—the ship, in this image—that makes it possible to land upon an island in the ocean of haqîqat. That island is none other than fotowwat.

Abraham was thus the initiator, the “father,” of all the mystical knights of faith (hence his titles: Arabic abû'l-fityân, Persian padar-e javânmardân). He became their father through a decision that anticipated the famous saying of the Sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sâdiq: “Islam began in exile, and it will become an exile again, as it was at the beginning. Blessed are those who go into exile for their faith.” Abraham's decision and Imam Ja'far's saying help us understand what it means for the pilgrims to sail toward the island of fotowwat.

Hoseyn Kâshefî writes: “Abraham was the first to choose to separate himself from this world and all its trappings, its vanities and sensual pleasures; to separate himself from the crowd and the tribe, to turn his back on his native land, and to bear the hardships and weariness of the pilgrim's journey and exile for God's sake”—for the javânmard is the pilgrim above all, our homo viator. “He had the courage to fight the idols, so much so that even his enemies paid tribute to his fotowwat: ‘We heard a young man (fatâ, a “knight”) speaking against our gods; they call him Abraham’ (Quran 21:61).

“Thus the original manifestation of fotowwat—both distinct from the path of Sufism and derived from it—was Abraham.” Our author adds: “This knowledge of fotowwat is a fragrance arising from the knowledge of the tarîqat.

“But many people, travellers out of the desert of heedlessness and unawareness, can hold on to nothing except words emptied of meaning. They put on the appearance of Ahl-e fotowwat”—people of spiritual chivalry, claiming to be knights of faith—“and pretend to know the inward truth (haqîqat) of this knowledge. That is why the sages placed a veil over it, to conceal it from the gaze of the uninitiated.”

The cycle of fotowwat inaugurated by Abraham takes the form of a transmission that crosses and intertwines with the transmission of the prophetic light (Nûr mohammadî), passing from prophet to prophet until it reaches the Seal of the Prophets and the complete assembly, or pleroma, of the twelve Imams. Abraham passes fotowwat to Ishmael and Isaac. From Isaac it passes to Jacob, and then through eminent figures whose names appear in both the Bible and the Quran—Joshua son of Nun, Joseph, and others. It passes through Christianity as well, particularly in the persons of the Seven Sleepers mentioned in the Quran (18:8–24).

The line of fotowwat follows the same rule as the line of gnosis (silsilat al-'irfân): it is never without someone to embody it in this world. It can dwell in a prophet or in a “Friend of God” (a walî, above all the Imam). When manifested in a prophet, it is handed on to that prophet's Imam.
Thus the Seal of the Prophets passed it on to Imam 'Alî.

The cycles of prophecy, walâyat or the Imamate, and fotowwat therefore overlap in the following way. The cycle of prophecy first appeared with Adam. Its pole was Abraham. Its Seal was the Prophet Muhammad, the “Seal of the Prophets.” Abraham, the pole of prophecy, inaugurated the cycle of fotowwat. The pole of fotowwat was the First Imam, 'Alî ibn Abî Tâlib. Its Seal is, and will be, the Twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Qâ'im, the Awaited One (montazar), the longed-for Imam, who is both present and, for now, invisible to human eyes.

The pole and the Seal of fotowwat are thus the very two figures of the Muhammadan Imamate who form the double Seal of the cycle of walâyat, the inward meaning of prophecy (bâtin al-nobowwat), whose cycle began with Seth. The pole of fotowwat is the First Imam, Seal of universal walâyat. The Seal of fotowwat is the Twelfth Imam, who is at the same time the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat. The three great moments of prophecy—Adam, Abraham, Muhammad—are matched by the three great moments of fotowwat: Abraham, the First Imam, the Twelfth Imam.

We learned earlier that all the prophets before Muhammad stood in relation to him, the Seal of Prophecy, as the Awliyâ, the “Friends of God” who come after the Seal of Prophecy, stand in relation to the Twelfth Imam.

It follows that this same relationship defines the place of all the spiritual knights, all the javânmardân, in relation to the Twelfth Imam, the Seal and final perfection of their fotowwat, their spiritual chivalry. This also reveals the bond between walâyat and fotowwat. The latter is the supreme manifestation of walâyat: it expresses walâyat as a way of life.

Each person, wherever he or she stands, is a companion of the Twelfth Imam; and this ethic makes each responsible for helping bring about his future appearance, the manifestation of the Imam as the Perfect Human Being. Spiritual chivalry (javânmardî, fotowwat) is therefore the ethic of the Friends of God (Awliyâ Allâh) in the cycle of walâyat, during this present period of “occultation.”

At this point it is hard not to hear an echo of the final message of Gottesfreundschaft, the friendship of God, entrusted to the Johannite knights of the Green Island. The bond of each javânmard with the Twelfth Imam likewise resembles the bond of each of Goethe's Rose Cross knights with Humanus, the Perfect Human Being who embodies the human condition in its full realization.

The Shiite idea of fotowwat, then, is of a community of javânmardân, or knights, embracing the entire Abrahamic tradition. Their archetype, the knight above all knights, is the Imam. One of the best-known hadiths repeats: “There is no knight but 'Alî, and no sword but Dhû'l-fiqâr”—the sword here symbolizing the power of interpretation that cuts through the obscurities of the Law taken only in its literal sense.

Since Abraham was the father of fotowwat, this tradition embraces the heroes of the Bible and the “Christian knights” represented by the Seven Sleepers mentioned in the Quran. In the West there is a corresponding ideal of an equally “ecumenical” chivalry, bringing together the knights of Christendom and of Islam. It finds its supreme expression in Wolfram von Eschenbach, for whom the heroic epic of the Knights Templar becomes the mystical epic of the Templars of the Grail. This transformation follows a path converging with the one taken by Suhrawardi, who also transformed the heroic epic into a mystical one.

Let us examine the horizon now opening before us, for it is ultimately this that can make the spiritual aspects of Iranian Islam mean something far more to us than a matter of archaeological or exotic interest.

We have already seen the first signs of this horizon in a conviction Shiism shares with the rest of Islam: the cycle of prophecy is closed. No prophet will come after the “Seal of Prophecy” has been sent into the world.

But Shiite feeling gives rise to an urgent, deeply troubled question: what becomes of humanity if, by its very nature and by the condition that makes it human, it cannot do without a prophet? The answer to this passionate question is the affirmation of the cycle of walâyat, inaugurated with the very closing of the cycle of prophecy. Our examination of fotowwat shows us what kind of human being the idea of walâyat calls upon us to become: a “Friend of God,” whose personal way of life, by that very fact, prepares the appearance of the Imam, the Perfect Human Being, as a divine manifestation.

As the cycle of initiation into the inward meaning of the prophetic message (bâtin al-nobowwat), the cycle of walâyat is also the cycle of fotowwat. Spiritual chivalry is that initiation into the secret of walâyat, the inner meaning of the Revelation communicated to the prophets. These knights, these javânmardân, form around the Imam, their spiritual centre, the silsilat al-'irfân, the unbroken line of gnosis, generation after generation. That line is “tradition” itself.

Yet everyone who joins it must undergo a new birth, so no one can use the authority of predecessors as an excuse for failing to be spiritually alive. This tradition is the very opposite of a funeral procession: it is perpetual rebirth. To join it is to enter the Malakût, the spiritual world. As a saying drawn directly from the Gospel of John declares—a saying our Shiite theosophers particularly love to quote—“No one can enter the Malakût unless born a second time.”

Though unknown to humanity, these “Friends of God” are the means by which it continues to exist, because through them the world of earthly human beings still communicates with the higher invisible world. This idea, and this ideal, are equally those of the disciples of the Friend of God of the Oberland and of the knights of the mystical Montserrat in Goethe's poem.

This implies a distinctive and exalted calling for the person we call a “philosopher.” This calling demands far more than we ordinarily associate with philosophy, and places upon the philosopher a responsibility more profound than any responsibility described today as “social.” We have seen this kind of philosopher—the theosophos, the sage of God—reveal the full meaning of his existence and his spiritual, cosmic role in Suhrawardi and the Illuminationists (Ishrâqîyûn).

We could already discern his emergence in Farabi and Avicenna, and it is among the Shiite theosophers that this ideal bears its fullest fruit. The whole of their metaphysics, and the understanding of human nature that follows from it, is directed toward one goal: the union of the human intellect—and, through it, of the whole inner person, the whole spiritual being—with what philosophers call the Active Intellect. They identify this Intellect with the Holy Spirit, the Angel Gabriel who brings revelation, the Angel of humanity.

We have explained how and why this identification of the Intellect with the Holy Spirit is entirely different from what some interpreters have understood as rationalism or intellectualism. In the mystery of this union, for which the theosopher prepares through sustained inner and intellectual discipline, the Angel-Intellect reveals itself to the mystic of Suhrawardi's tradition as the “Perfect Nature,” the personal Angel, in all the variations of this theme found in gnosis—and ultimately as the Imam, the personal guide.

However we explain or imagine this mystical union, it is through that very union that communication remains open between our world and the higher world of the Malakut, the spiritual realm. Through it, humanity itself continues to exist. This, in turn, is what defines the knightly service of the philosopher as a sage of God and makes him a javanmard, a spiritual knight, in the fullest sense. Such is the philosopher as conceived by the Illuminationists and the Shiite theosophers.

This philosopher is certainly something other, and something more, than the word “philosopher” usually suggests to us. We recognize that additional dimension when we find ourselves obliged to describe his philosophy as prophetic philosophy, because of the role he assumes in the cycle of walayat—the cycle of spiritual initiation and divine friendship that follows the cycle of prophecy. He is a sage of God, a theosophos. He is guided by the Active Intellect, with which he becomes united at the highest point of knowing.

And at the summit of his own faculties there is what the tradition calls the intellectus sanctus, the holy intellect, upon which the Angel pours its light—the Angel who is at once the Angel of knowledge and the Angel of revelation. It is through this that the philosopher can enter the sanctuary of divine wisdom and pass beyond the ordinary horizon of philosophy. For the philosopher, to explore the world of the Intellects is to explore the world brought into existence by the divine Command and, through that world, to know the Source from which it emanates.

But we have seen that for the Shiite theosopher, beyond the horizon of the first Being—the first to be brought into existence—lies the unfathomable mystery of the Absconditum, the hidden God who can be approached only through negative theology, which recognizes the inadequacy of everything we can say about the divine. We have seen that the secret of the Muhammadan Light, the Haqîqat mohammadîya, is the manifestation of this hidden God as Deus revelatus, God revealed: the mystery of the theophany, or divine self-manifestation. And the mystery of this divine Face revealed to humanity is precisely the mystery of the Imam and the Imamate.

Guided by the secret of its teaching about the Imam, Shiite theosophy has carried the metaphysics of being higher—or further—than what is called “absolute” being, because the absolute itself implies the mystery of its own Absolvens, that which releases or makes it absolute. The mystery within the divine of this “absolution” of being is the passage from the hidden God to God revealed. This is the divine gift bestowed upon theosophy as the fulfillment of prophetic philosophy.

At every level we have briefly recalled, the philosopher-theosopher performs the service of a spiritual knight—a javanmard in the fullest sense—because it is through him that these realities continue to have meaning for human beings and continue to concern them. Just as every prophet is called a fatâ, a knight of faith, and his struggle was the struggle of such a knight, so too, without the prophetic philosophy of these theosophers, humanity would become permanently deaf and blind, deprived of every memory of its own preexistent being.

The loss of this inner vision and this memory is the inverted, satanic “service” performed by a philosophy stripped of its sacred character and secularized. Prophetic philosophy, by contrast, affirms a calling shared by prophet and philosopher. The Angel pours its illumination upon the same intellectus sanctus in both.

Thus the philosopher finds himself at home in the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world: the realm of individual, concrete spiritual realities where the visions of the prophets unfold and where the secrets of worlds and intermediary worlds, eternally present, are inscribed. This is possible because, for the philosopher of prophetic philosophy, the intellect and the imagination communicate through that same holy intellect.

His experience of divine wisdom is therefore no longer expressed in doctrine alone. Doctrine becomes an actual event in the soul. The theosopher becomes the javanmard, the knight of the mystical epic. This is what Suhrawardi's work has enabled us to understand. His mystical narratives stand between the great spiritual epics of Hakim Sana'i and Attar. These narratives and epics—the events whose stories they tell—must therefore be read as revealing the inner, esoteric meaning of a doctrine that, by comparison, still remained at the level of its literal meaning. All too often, we read them the other way around.

The hidden meaning of the events lies higher than the doctrines. It is their personal fulfillment, the truth attained at the end of the quest: the haqîqat. Such is the mystical epic of the spiritual knight. Suhrawardi showed us its source in the Xvarnah, the Mazdaean Light of Glory. We have seen how an inspired hadith finds an echo of this in Sufism, when it salutes Zoroaster as the prophet of the religion of love.

Suhrawardi performed a spiritual knight's service by bringing the Hellenized Magi back into Islamic Persia and leading the “Greek prophets”—the Neoplatonists—back to the “Niche of Lights” of prophecy (mishkât al-nobowwat). The theosopher is thus the knight of a mystical epic in which humanity is raised toward its origin, the origin that sets it free. To “advance” toward that origin is to leave, as Abraham did, the land of one's birth, which is the world of exile.
It was to this epic that an entire spiritual knighthood was called: a knighthood of faith, participating in the Abrahamic tradition.

This explains the correspondences we can discern, for example, between Shiite and Jewish theosophy: in their conception of the philosopher who takes up the message of the prophets; in their recognition that this philosopher has an indispensable role in preserving humanity; and in the distinction they draw between a theosophy established from the outset upon the spiritual interpretation of the Holy Book and a philosophy initially concerned with developing the Neoplatonic inheritance. I do not claim the competence here to discuss the relations between the Kabbalah and philosophy.
Nevertheless, certain parallels that suggest themselves cannot be passed over in silence.

For Shiite theosophy, beyond the pleroma, or fullness, of the Intellects lies the pleroma of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones, the fullness of the Muhammadan Reality (Haqîqat mohammadîya). This is the receptive aspect (absolutum) of the active divine Command that brings things into existence. As such, it is the primordial absolute being called into existence by that Command, the Absolvens.

Is the Light of Lights itself the supreme Principle, as the Illuminationist philosophers believe? Or is it, as the Muhammadan Light, the first being summoned into existence by the Command of the hidden God—the KN, the divine “Be!” (Esto)? A similar question arises in Jewish Kabbalah because certain philosophers identify the pleroma of the Intellects with the series of Sephirot, understood as Deus revelatus, God revealed. Is the Infinite (En Sof) identical with the first of the Sephirot, the Crown, or does it remain distinct from it?

We can do no more than raise the question here. It calls for a comparative study of theosophy that has scarcely begun. We mention it because the thinkers for whom, and through whom, such a question arises—at one time or another—belong to the same kind of philosophical tradition in which the study of prophecy and the meaning of philosophy have appeared inseparable. In such a tradition, every precise boundary between philosophy and theosophy disappears: neither can do without the other.

To profess, for example, as certain Jewish theosophers do, that prophecy includes “speculative perceptions” is already to affirm that the true prophet must necessarily be an authentic philosopher as well. Once again, this presupposes the illuminating action of the Angel who is simultaneously the Angel of knowledge and the Angel of revelation. The Active Intellect may pour its illumination upon the human intellect alone, as in the case of purely speculative philosophers.

Or it may illuminate both the intellect and the imaginative faculty, as in the case of the prophet who is at once a consummate metaphysician and divinely inspired. This is also the case of the Perfect Sage according to Suhrawardi, the master of both speculative wisdom and ta'alloh, the spiritual experience of the divine. Suhrawardi describes this same Sage, in Zoroastrian terminology, as invested with the royal Xvarnah, the Light of Glory, and as the pole of humanity, whether visible or hidden.

Jewish theosophy likewise affirms that the survival of the human species requires a joining or union of the Active Intellect with the human intellect. The existence of the Perfect Human Being, in whom this union takes place, is therefore indispensable to the very continuance of the world. This is exactly what Shiite theosophy teaches about the Imam as the spiritual pole, “since it is in his person that the higher world and the lower world meet.” Abraham is offered as an example of such a person: one whom his people recognized as a “divine prince.”

This teaching corresponds not only to what Suhrawardi says about the Perfect Sage, but also to the central theme of the First Imam's conversation with his disciple Komayl ibn Ziyad. In that conversation, the unbroken lineage—the “tradition”—of spiritual knowledge (silsilat al-'irfân) is solemnly affirmed. Because this lineage is precisely what secures the continued existence of humanity, it constitutes the highest form of fotowwat, spiritual knighthood, throughout the cycle of walayat.

On both sides, the same spiritual journey leads the theosophers to recognize in prophetic inspiration and philosophical illumination the work of one and the same Angel: the Angel of intellectual understanding for the philosopher and the Angel of inspiration for the prophet. The divine prophetic influence flows to the prophets through the same Angel-Intellect that pours intelligible truths into the philosopher's intellect. And just as Shiite theosophy draws its nourishment from the Holy Book and the hadiths that disclose the Book's hidden meanings, so for these metaphysicians of prophetic philosophy the masters are Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Zechariah.

In the words of the prophet Zechariah, “the angel who speaks within me” (VI, 4), the theosopher recognizes that “when prophetic inspiration rests upon the prophet, the prophet and the angel speaking within him become one”. This is a mystical union, an unio mystica, occurring in the prophet just as it occurs in the philosopher-theosopher who speaks of the union of the soul with the Active Intellect. The Intelligence that brings his potential intellect into full actuality is the very same Angel who “speaks within the prophet.”

This is why, among these prophetic philosophers, the union of the Active Intellect with the soul, contemplated through the visions granted to the prophets, was itself expressed as a vision. Its language possesses a beauty surpassing even that of the finest mystical epics, for the supreme union it announces is also the fulfillment toward which those epics lead. The theosophers of the Bible gave this union its own name: the “kiss of the seraph.” Isaiah's vision becomes a vision of this union and then continues into the musical cadences of the Song of Songs.

Let us listen to one of these theosophers meditating upon Isaiah's vision (VI, 1 ff.), in which the seraph flies toward the prophet and touches his mouth with a burning coal. Here the seraph represents the Intellect, the Angel who stands last in the hierarchy of the separate Intellects, and therefore nearest to humanity. In this tradition the Angel is called Michael rather than Gabriel, as he is among the philosophers of Islam. “One of the seraphim flew toward me ... Here is Michael, one of the seraphim, coming to my aid.

“In his hand is a burning coal.” Such, indeed, is the condition of the human intellect in relation to the Active Intellect at the moment when the human intellect becomes an intellect in act, capable of understanding the Angel and joining itself to him. “He touched his mouth and said: See, this has touched your lips; your sin has departed.” “When Isaiah understood the form of the Union, he joined himself to the angel in a union that might more properly be called a transformation into a single being.”
